opus-5.5.text:
You know, I think it's actually a return to Silicon Valley's roots. If you go back to the early days, to Hewlett and Packard in the garage, to the Traitorous Eight leaving Shockley to start Fairchild, and then Intel, these were deeply technical people. They were engineers and physicists who understood the technology at a very fundamental level, and that understanding let them see what was possible before anyone else did.

Then for a period, especially during the consumer internet and mobile era, the technology became somewhat commoditized. You could build a great web or mobile app without deep technical insight, and the differentiator was often go-to-market, design, or business model innovation. Those things still matter a lot, of course.

But with AI, we're in a moment where the technology is changing so rapidly that the technical understanding really matters again. If you're building an AI application, you need a gut-level sense of what models can and can't do today, what they'll likely be able to do in six months, and how to architect agentic workflows, evaluations, and so on. Someone who has that intuition can make decisions in an hour that might take a less technical team weeks, or that they'd get wrong entirely.

At AI Fund, one thing I've seen is that the fastest-moving teams are almost always led by people who are technical, or at least who have invested heavily in understanding the technology. Speed of execution is a huge predictor of startup success, and technical depth is a big driver of speed right now.

That said, I don't think it's either/or. The best founders I work with combine technical depth with a real obsession with customers. And I'm encouraged that the tools are getting good enough that more people can become technical. I really think everyone should learn to code, especially now with AI coding assistants, because it lets more people participate in this wave the way those early engineers participated in the semiconductor wave.

r001.rationale: The response calls the emphasis a return to Silicon Valley’s roots and describes early founders such as Hewlett, Packard, and the Fairchild Eight as deeply technical.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think it's actually a return to the roots of Silicon Valley. If you go back to the early history, this place was built by engineers. Hewlett and Packard were engineers. The founders of Fairchild, the people who went on to start Intel, these were deeply technical people. Silicon Valley got its name from the silicon, from the semiconductor engineers who were building things with their hands and their understanding of physics.

Somewhere along the way, maybe in the last fifteen or twenty years, there was a period where it felt like a business background and a good go-to-market story could carry a company pretty far. And that worked for a while, because a lot of the technology was relatively mature. If you were building a SaaS application, the technical risk was lower, and the harder question was distribution.

But what I see now with AI is that we're back in a phase where the technology is moving so fast that the technical insight is the competitive advantage. The question of what is actually possible this month, versus what was possible six months ago, is changing all the time. And if you don't have someone on the founding team who deeply understands the technology, you don't even know what to build. You'll either be too ambitious and build something the technology can't support yet, or you'll be too timid and build something that a foundation model will make obsolete in three months.

So I tell people, especially at AI Fund where we build companies, that the ideal founder today looks a lot like the founders from the 1960s and 70s. Someone who can look at a new capability and immediately see ten applications, and also knows which three of those ten are actually feasible. That kind of judgment only comes from really understanding the technology hands-on. I don't think that's a new idea. I think it's a very old idea that we're rediscovering.

r001.rationale: The response calls the emphasis on technical founders a return to Silicon Valley’s roots and describes its early founders as engineers and deeply technical people.

astra-6.text:
I think, in some ways, it’s a return to Silicon Valley’s roots. If you think about the early semiconductor companies, the founders were deeply technical people. They understood the technology, and that understanding let them see opportunities that weren’t obvious to everyone else.

With AI, I think that matters a lot again. The technology is changing so quickly that understanding what you can build—and what you can’t yet build—is a real advantage. A technical founder can have an idea, build something, learn from it, and iterate without needing a large team to get started.

That doesn’t mean the business side goes away. You still need to understand customers and distribution. But I see technical depth and customer understanding as complementary. The exciting founders are the ones who can connect a new technical capability to a problem people actually need solved.

r001.rationale: The response calls the emphasis a return to Silicon Valley’s roots and says early semiconductor founders were deeply technical.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Silicon Valley has a long history of technical founders. If you look back at the semiconductor industry, a lot of the people building those companies had a very deep understanding of the technology. And that mattered because understanding what was technically possible helped them see opportunities that weren’t obvious to everyone else.

I think AI creates a similar dynamic. The technology is changing so quickly that being able to build something yourself, experiment, and understand where it works and where it fails is a real advantage. You can go from an idea to a prototype and learn from customers much faster.

That doesn’t mean the technology alone makes a business. You still need to understand customers, distribution, and all the other things that make a company successful. But I see the emphasis on technical founders as quite consistent with Silicon Valley’s roots.

r001.rationale: The response says technical founders are consistent with Silicon Valley’s roots and supports this by describing technically expert founders in the early semiconductor industry.
